t: LeetCode 2242 - Maximum Score of a Node Sequence: Top-3 Neighbor Pruning
o: **Understanding the problem.** A valid sequence is a chain of exactly four distinct nodes x1-x2-x3-x4 joined by three edges; we maximize the sum of their scores. Every candidate is fully determined by its middle edge (x2, x3) plus one neighbor x1 of x2 and one neighbor x4 of x3, with all four nodes distinct. In example 1, the middle edge (1, 2) with x1 = 0 and x4 = 3 yields 5 + 2 + 9 + 8 = 24. Trying every neighbor pair per edge costs the product of the endpoint degrees and blows past the limits when a high-degree hub meets many edges. The fix: only the three highest-scoring neighbors of each endpoint can ever matter, shrinking each edge check to at most nine pairs.
k: A length-4 sequence is assembled around its middle edge; both endpoints hang off that edge.
For a fixed middle edge, an arm has at most two forbidden node values, so among the top-3 scored neighbors at least one is always usable.
Capping every adjacency list at its 3 best entries turns the whole search into linear work after preprocessing.

a.n: Approach 1: Middle Edge Times All Neighbor Pairs (Brute Force)
a.i: Build adjacency lists, then treat every edge as the middle pair and try each neighbor of one endpoint against each neighbor of the other, skipping any repeats of the middle nodes or of each other. Simple and obviously correct, but a hub of degree D makes its incident edges cost O(D) or worse each, degrading toward quadratic time on dense stars.
s: For each edge `(a, b)`, iterate `c` over neighbors of `a` with `c != b`.
Iterate `d` over neighbors of `b` with `d` not in `{a, b, c}`.
Track the maximum of `scores[a] + scores[b] + scores[c] + scores[d]`; return -1 if never updated.
a.t: O(sum over edges of deg(u)*deg(v)) - up to O(E^2) on hub-heavy graphs, too slow at the limits.

a.n: Approach 2: Keep Top-3 Scored Neighbors per Node
a.i: Preprocess each node into its three highest-scoring neighbors stored as (score, node) pairs. Three entries suffice because, once the middle edge is fixed, an arm may be blocked only by the opposite middle node and by the other arm choice - at most two forbidden values - so some entry of the top-3 is always legal. Each edge is then settled by at most nine pairings, making the main loop effectively linear.
s: For each node, collect `(score[neighbor], neighbor)` for all neighbors.
Keep only the 3 largest entries by score.
For each edge `(a, b)`, try all `(c, d)` from top[a] x top[b], skipping when `c == b` or `d` equals `a`, `b`, or `c`.
Update the answer with the four scores; return it, or -1 if no valid pairing exists.
a.t: O(E log V) - sorting degree-sized lists during preprocessing dominates; the scan is O(9E).
a.sp: O(V + E) - trimmed top-3 neighbor lists.

w: Lead with the middle-edge decomposition - stating it crisply is most of the solution. Pitfalls: forgetting that the two arm choices must also differ from each other (both arms can see the same high-scoring node), and assuming top-1 per node suffices when the single best neighbor can collide with the opposite arm. Likely follow-ups: generalize to sequences of length L (keep top-(L-2) neighbors), or handle negative scores where the pruning argument needs care.
